utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning. After I looked through the transcript, I should like to make some corrections which, it seems to me, to be important to begin with. I didn't give a proper answer to Judge May's question about the place where the film was shot, the soldiers with ribbons. I tried to check out the date, but all we have is information on the film, and that is the 20th of April, 1993. That is all that we know about it. But I'm told that this is a fragment of a two-hour video cassette with a number of short films which make part of the HVO propaganda. Of this two-hour videotape, we have already shown a number of films, and particularly I'm sure Your Honours will remember showing soldiers going through Ahmici before the conflict of the 16th of April, 1993, and that was Exhibit 354 [incorrect interpretation]. The cassette was given to the Defence, and they also used it. That is all that I know about this tape. I can only add that it was by a person from Zenica who turned it over to the Tribunal in 1997. Then on page 11451 of the transcript, I asked the witness, and I believe it was improperly translated or at least not fully properly translated, the transcript says that I asked the witness, it was Witness B, and I shall not mention the name because we are in open session, why did he say that he saw at his place a rifle, helmet, and a package of ammunition. I was talking about a military kit, military bag or something like that, I don't know how one translates, but it's not the ammunition. At any rate, on page 11486, I asked the witness to confirm, and the witness confirmed, said that he left the depression to go see his house on the 19th of April, 1993, and I was talking about the 18th of April, 1993, and the witness was referred to the 18th of April, not the 19th. Those were the corrections that I wish to make. Yes, Mr. President, somebody said that I talked about -- that the exhibit is not 354 but 352. That is the tape. I will begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning. Witness, we shall resume, if you please, where we left off yesterday, and that is the question when did you realise and understand what had been going on in Ahmici in the morning of the 16th of April? You told us yesterday, and I reread your statement carefully, that during the first hours, you thought that the Mujahedin were attacking the village and that fighting was going on. Later on, you said that you realised that it was Muslim houses which were on fire, and you discovered that Muslim civilians were the victims and that they were being killed. But you also added that you thought that the combat, that some of the fighting continuing. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, some you did understand and some, I believe, was misinterpreted because I said that during the first few hours, I realised that fighting was going on up there and that the fire came from both sides. After my first departure to see my family and return, I could see in the direction of Zume, towards the main road, some Muslim houses burning, and also I learned that several people were killed down there. I didn't say whether they were civilians or soldiers because I did not know what they were. After I learned from my relative, Ivica, that it was Muslim houses burning, not ours, that was information which told me that it was the Muslims who were the victims, and I still did not know whether they were civilians or soldiers or how or in what way, but to my mind, fighting was going on. In the evening, before it went dark, around the mosque, around the mosque, what was going on around the mosque was fighting. However, I say that even today, I still do not know who attacked whom and how, and I can only conclude from results that I learned later on and saw that it was, indeed, the Muslims who were victimised there, and their houses had burnt down and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Why is it that you think that in the afternoon of the 16th of April, in particular, around their mosque, the fighting was going on? Were you observing the situation at the time? Did you hear something at the time? Did you see anything? Were you told something? What was it that led you to believe that fighting was going on around the mosque in the afternoon of the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We saw no detonations, but since the gunfire was intensive, we were hiding in the same place down there, and a detonation came some half an hour later, approximately, I'm saying. There was fierce fighting on both sides because some bullets even hit the wood where we were, that is, from the other side. After that half hour of that very intensive gunfire, it abated and we heard a detonation, and the minaret of the mosque went down. We did not see the exact moment when it was demolished, but in view of the detonation and the cessation of gunfire, we could take a peek between the tree trunks to come up, and we could see the fire next to the mosque and we could not see the minaret anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, but my question was slightly different. I wanted to know, on the basis of which information or which observation did you think that the fighting was still going on around the mosque in the village of Ahmici or anywhere in Ahmici in the afternoon of the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not referring to afternoon hours. I'm talking about the evening, about 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening. After UNPROFOR left the village, that was around noon, perhaps around 12.00 or perhaps 1.00, the gunfire continued after that, but it was intermittent and it wasn't as intensive as it was in the morning. That gunfire, at around 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening, was just as intensive as in the morning. Well, I can't claim, but it was much more intensive than a tiny moment after the departure of the UNPROFOR. Again, I say it was around 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening, and the bullets were flying around. I mean, it seemed to us that they were very near us, but they could have been very far away, but we felt them coming from the other side, and that is why I concluded that it was a full-scale combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, we heard different Defence witnesses who told us here that at 1.00 -- that at a particular time on the 16th of April, and I'm not mentioning any hour, Vlatko Kupreskic left Ivica's shelter and went home. On the 16th of April, was it in the morning or in the afternoon? I mean, this is something that can be discussed at some other time. So is it that Vlatko Kupreskic went back home on the 16th of April, either towards the late morning or in the afternoon, it doesn't really matter, and you did not go back to your house, only on the 18th of April? Why could Vlatko Kupreskic do that and you didn't?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps Vlatko is braver than I am. I don't know. Vinko Sakic told us that Vlatko had been to his place. I did not see him. I do not know when it was that Vlatko went home. Whether simply the anxiety about his father, who had stayed at home, prevailed on him, I really don't know. But what I knew about the burning of Muslim houses, what I knew about the Muslim houses around our houses burning, I simply wasn't thinking about my own house. With all those houses on fire, I never thought about my house. Besides, I had no particular valuables in that house, apart from the house itself, because we had not even moved into it yet. Only two rooms were inhabitable at the time. When I saw all that, I never thought about my house. I simply didn't care about it. I cared about my family, about my wife, about three small children, and my own life. What Vlatko thought at the time, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You are telling us that somebody told you that he saw Vlatko Kupreskic, but this is not mentioned in the transcript. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Niko Sakic told us that Vlatko had gone to his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: It was then that he told you, when you were in the depression, not on some other day? It was then that he told you that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 16th, in the afternoon, Niko Sakic came to see us on several occasions, and on one of those occasions when he came, on the 16th, in the afternoon of the 16th, he told us that Vlatko had been to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember saying during your examination that that day you called Ivan Josipovic, who was a friend of yours. Do you remember saying that during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I called on the 17th. I don't remember if it was in the morning when I went to see my family or in the afternoon, and I said that I called several persons that morning, not only Ivan Josipovic but Zdravo Matkovic and [redacted], and I tried to call some others, I couldn't get through, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, who is Ivan Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ivan Josipovic is a worker like Zdravo Matkovic. They also worked with me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: At that moment, was he a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you know a Ivan Josipovic who was a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know another Ivan Josipovic who worked for the civilian police. I believe he was a judge or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But they are not one and the same person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You spoke about Nikola Omazic and other witnesses. You remember that during that debate we had the opportunity of looking at a document showing that Nikola Omazic had been wounded that 16th of April in Ahmici while he fought in the ranks of the Vitez Brigade. When you saw Nikola Omazic, did you understand that he was a member of the Vitez Brigade, that he was in Ahmici in order to participate in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could never say that of Omazic and I could never interpret it that way because I saw him without a uniform with a rifle. He never stood guard with us, and I just don't know where he was. I know that he was a man prone to drinking. I don't think he was a serious enough man to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember that document or would you like me to -- that military document, do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that document, and I learnt on the 17th that Nikola had been wounded in the afternoon of the 16th, but I learned that from Mirko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Before I change the subject, I should like to ask you another question referring to Nikola Santic, Mirjan Santic, and perhaps some others. When you reflect on that day of the 16th of April, don't you have a feeling that the aggressor was perfectly informed about the topography of Ahmici and its villagers, that is, who lived in which house? We know that amongst Muslim and Croat houses, there is a traditional difference, but we also saw that there were some exceptions to that, yet the aggressor did not make a mistake. Don't you have a feeling, don't you think that the aggressor must have been accompanied by persons from the inside from the village who took part in the aggression? Have you ever reflected about -- did you ever give it a thought?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I could make some guesses or speculate or think about this, but about some of Kupreskics' houses: Our houses are not mixed with the Muslim houses. As you go from Zume towards Ahmici by our houses, the last Croat houses are ours and the following houses are all Muslim. Secondly, if it were so, such a large number of people know that, not only from Ahmici. It could be from a border area, from Santici and other places. Very many people are aware of the situation. Perhaps in some other places, it is not like that, perhaps they are mixed and they alternate perhaps, but in our case, that is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I simply thought, for instance, I had in mind Fahrudin's house. That was a rectangular house near Josipovics' house, yet the aggressors never made a mistake; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said I don't know. It's down by the road. And I said that down there, there are some houses which are mixed, but that is not the case with my house or our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I believe you said, but I don't have the exact reference, I think this was yesterday or the day after yesterday or, rather, on Friday, sorry, that around your house, the Kupreskic houses, you saw, on the 18th of April, two Muslim houses which were still intact; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Whose houses were they?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I remember, these houses are intact to this day. This is a new house under a roof belonging to Semsudin Ahmic, a son, and a new house belonging to the son of Mehmed Krdzalic. I don't know his name. I believe he lived in Austria or somewhere outside and he was building the house there. From what I know, those houses were never damaged. In addition to those, Bilics' and Strmonjes' houses in Zume.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: These houses which you are referring, which were still intact, were they habitable and inhabited on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Krdzalic's son's house, no, it was not habitable, and Semsudin Ahmic's house, well, perhaps one room could be used, but I'm not sure. So it's quite possible that one room was habitable, but don't take my word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you are not disputing the fact that in your particular area, around your house, around Kupreskics' houses, all the Muslim houses, that is, those which were habitable and inhabitable, were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Now I should like to talk to you about the family of (redacted. Could you tell us, on what kind of terms were you with her family?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I only met late (redacted) of that whole family and we would greet. I don't think that I met his wife more than on a couple of occasions. And children, I don't think I ever saw them. Perhaps they were playing with other children but I didn't realise they were (redacted) children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You are talking about (redacted), about the father of the family who was killed on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Is it true that (redacted) was in the car repair business?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he was into that because he had his shop registered. I'm not sure whether it was registered, but I know that he was into that business.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Have you been to their house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I've never visited their house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Have you ever been to (redacted)'s car repair shop?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I said already I've never in my life been to that house or that shop, not even near that house, although my house is relatively near, but I've never been to that house or even in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What is the distance between his house and your house, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: His house is some 30 or 40 metres from his father's, Sakib's house, further than my own, that is, down there towards the road. First comes Sakib's house, then his yard, then the stable, and after that is (redacted) house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But you told us that you were on very good terms with (redacted), his house is 60 or 80 metres from yours, and yet you never went to see him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I didn't say I was on very good terms with him. We were on neighbourly terms, "Hi." "Hi." "How are you?" "How are you?" That was about it. But I never paid him a visit nor did he ever come to see me at my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should now like to refer to testimony in a private session, please. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: 1 (redacted) 2 (redacted) 3 (redacted) 4 (redacted) 5 (redacted) 6 (redacted) 7 (redacted) 8 (redacted) 9 (redacted) 10 (redacted) 11 (redacted) 12 (redacted) 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, you remember [redacted] [redacted] There again, since you heard all of them, you heard all of his testimony and you heard that he pointed to you and your brother in a very specific and accurate way, and he pointed to you both as being the perpetrators of the death of the four people in his family who were in the house at the time. What did [redacted] statement arouse in you in terms of thinking?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It makes me think that due to this statement, I have suffered a lot throughout this time, but what can I do? I was not there, and we had an opportunity to see that what I'm talking about now is the same thing that that witness also testified to, at least in the first several statements. But as things developed, as things evolved, at first, he was in a hospital, and then when he was able to exchange stories and points of view, and this is just my own point of view, then I think that he came to the idea that he should not point to somebody who came from Busovaca or from somewhere else. He may have said, "Well, I know Zoran and Mirjan, and I'll say that." This is what I'm guessing, obviously, and I have no proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what kind of terms you were on with that family before the 16th of April, 1993? Were you on good terms with Sakib Ahmic, but also with his children and grandchildren or, let's say, his children?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My God, these were just normal, regular relationships. I lived there for 30 years. Those relationships did not change a single bit until that situation which was around in those days. We would greet each other, and we did that a couple of days before that as well as 15 years before that, we would greet each other in the say way. I would see Sakib. I would greet him. I knew Naser, and Naser was even closer to my brother Mirjan. I didn't know the children and the grandchildren. I saw those children all mingled together, and I didn't know whose were whose. The children would just play, and we would not exchange any greetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the grandchildren. Let us talk about Naser Ahmic. Did you just say that you were on friendly terms with him? Could you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said I had friendly relations, amicable relations with everyone. Naser did not stand out in relation to (redacted) or (redacted), the other two brothers. I just know that my brother worked at the Sutra company, and he would see Naser more often. Also, they are of the same generation. He is not of my generation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: But, for instance, would Naser go to your house or did you go to his house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, Naser never came to my house, and he did not have his own house. He lived with his father, so I couldn't go there myself. But as far as Sakib's house is concerned, I was there a few times as a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, as an adult, you never went to Naser and Sakib Ahmic's house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you know, even if you never went to their house, where exactly Sakib lived? Where did he live in that house? Which was his room? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I knew that Sakib lived in the house. I knew that he had problems with his wife, that they had separated. Then here I learned that he got the basement and that the top part of the house was his wife's, and I don't know exactly where he was, where he lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Therefore, prior to the 16th of April, you thought that Sakib Ahmic lived in the cellar of that house; is that what you thought?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know. I said that I didn't know because I saw him by his house. When he was going into his garden, he would emerge into the garden both from underneath and from the top of the house, so I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness, we are in a public hearing now. I'm not going to mention the name of this person. This is a friend of yours in Vitez, a friend of yours who used to live in Vitez. She stated in paragraph 26 of the said statement, she said the following, and I'd like to know from you whether this statement is accurate. She said the following: "Zoran told me that he had been threatened by them, the Jokers, in Ahmici on the morning of the attack. After removing his family and parents from Ahmici, he returned to Ahmici and joined soldiers in the trenches." I will go on. "They," the soldiers, I suppose, "were firing at Muslim civilians who were trying to run away. One of the Jokers noticed that Zoran was not firing. He put a gun to his temple and said, 'If you don't shoot the civilians, I will kill you.' Zoran told them he couldn't shoot at these people because he knew them. He went back to the trench and pretended to shoot at them, but actually he was firing shots in the air." Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. If you want me to, I can say what I told her, and I don't know how then from there she may have construed the story as she did, but that's not how I told her what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what may have caused such confusion in this person's mind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. The only thing I can think of is that she wanted to help me by giving such a statement, but I know that on the 18th of April, in Upper Pirici, I was forced to dig a trench. There was no pistol pointed to my temple. Mirko Sakic and I both dug, as well as the others around us. I did not mention to [redacted] the Jokers, nor did I see them there because there was the military police present. As far as the civilians and shooting is concerned, I did not see a single civilian, nor did anybody shoot at civilians there while I was there. Perhaps this story may be linked to Zume. When some people were brought there, the military policemen shot over their heads, trying to scare them into going back home. So this may have been construed by [redacted], but I don't know what she may now confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We will see that later, since she's going to be summoned as a prosecution witness. This same person stated in paragraph 31, and now she was talking about a much later time, following the time when you were indicted. She met you then in 1994, and according to her, you asked her whether she was willing to provide an alibi to you that would say that you were at her place at the time of the attack, and she said that there was no way that could be accepted; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not even remotely so. First of all, in 1994, there was no indictment; that was in 1996. It was in 1996 when we got together. We were in Ljilja's apartment. Second, I would have been crazy if I had suggested something like that. I was an innocent person, so why would I have asked for such a thing? I could have just said that I was with my wife in the shelter. So I never suggested anything like that. I only asked her whether she was prepared, if this would be necessary, because I still did not believe that it would come to this, to write down what happened. She was still not prepared at that time to testify, but she was prepared to make a written statement. At first, she didn't dare. First, she wanted to write it down and then sign it, and then later on, she didn't want that either. There were Muslim colleagues of hers who were in Zenica, and I also asked her whether she could ask them whether they, these colleagues of mine, would also say something, give some statements, and she promised that she would try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness. I would like -- I think I made a mistake. I want to check that. Exhibits 375 and 376 have already been admitted into evidence. I have one last little problem. During the cross-examination, I did not mention the written statement by Fuad Berbic. Does that mean that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: There is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: There doesn't seem to be a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said. During the cross-examination, I did not use the written statement made by one of the witnesses for whom the Court had kindly agreed to me using the statement. Does that mean that the Prosecution does not have to call that witness as a witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You mean Fuad Berbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have one question. Given that the Prosecution had the permission of the Trial Chamber to quote certain excerpts from the statement, does the Defence have the same right? This is in reference to the statement of Fuad Berbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether actually the Prosecutor quoted from this statement. I think he didn't quote anything from this particular statement. In this case, you would not be authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That is correct. He did not quote anything from the statement, but we also believe that he had the right to use certain statements and elicit comments from the witness on them. So we also believe that it would be useful for ascertaining the truthfulness of certain portions of the statement, in other words, just to make statements, I would not quote them, but I would just like to elicit comments on certain points from these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, allow me a very brief comment following what Mrs. Glumac said. I did not use, I did not mention the statement, as the Defence just said. Therefore, it seems somewhat strange that, during the redirect examination, a statement which was not used previously, neither in the examination-in-chief, nor in the cross-examination, should be used. I am only referring to the general rules applied here in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the Prosecutor is right. Could you please refrain from quoting from this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, tell me, first of all, in relation to some of these statements that you made to the Prosecutor, I'm just going to ask you a few questions by way of additional clarification. Tell us, when you said that you worked in the folklore society, you said that you were not paid by anyone for your performances, and that for a given time you, as a society, had sponsors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you performed on Bajram on the 24th of March, 1993, was that paid for by a Muslim organisation or did they organise everything that had to do with your performance, that is to say, at least to cover your costs, if not give you a fee?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In most cases, we only had costs to cover. The only things we got was perhaps having a glass of juice for the children, perhaps having a drink, having a bite to eat. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about your performance for Bajram. Did anybody pay for anything?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no one paid anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you were not financially motivated at all to perform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that you tried, after the war, to contact persons who were members of your folklore society, Napredak, and you wanted to get them back so that you could restart, and you mentioned some names, including Ahmet Delic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that he had joined you. Could you tell us what he is by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ahmet Delic is of Muslim faith. I only realised then that his mother was from Ahmici. I didn't know that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did Ahmet Delic make a statement in connection with your character?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, precisely what I asked [redacted] to do and some others, those who dared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor mentioned, in connection with the military document that was presented to you concerning the analysis of your personality which was obviously made by a military security service, the Prosecutor mentioned a change in your position in November 1993. Could you briefly describe the military situation in Vitez in the second half of 1993, not to say the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know you that could not get out of Vitez. Croats were surrounded by Muslim forces all around. We were in trenches, and we responded to various attacks only by infantry fire. I did not have the opportunity to do so very often but others did. In Krizancevo Selo, at the end of the year, there were over 80 dead. Soon afterwards, Bucici Kuce, the same. In a word, terrible. My wife and children were just a few kilometres behind me, and my mother and father were only 500 metres behind me. Could anyone have gotten out, I think they all would have, but it was impossible to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In that area, after the war started and after that part of the Lasva River Valley was encircled by the Muslims, was there any other way out for the Croats there, except to fight?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have any other way out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Had I had another way out, I would have made use of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What would you have made use of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm trying to say that had I had any other way out, I would have resorted to it. On the 16th, 17th, 18th, the only thing -- I only did what I thought was good and reasonable to do. Had I had any other options, I would have done that. Zoran Kupreskic did that. I don't know what else I could have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, to the best of your knowledge, when did a person become a member of the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A person becomes a member of the reserve force in the age span from 18 to 60 in the former Yugoslav People's Army. In the former Yugoslav People's Army, all the time one spent outside the Yugoslav People's Army, and apart from the period when you were mobilised, you are a military-aged and military-able man, but you're a member of the reserve. So if you're mobilised, you're a soldier, and if you are not mobilised, you are a civilian, but you are part of the reserve force. So we were all part of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So a person who is in the reserve force is a civilian. Does such a person go to one's regular work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If this person has a job, then that that person goes to work. It depends on whether this person has a job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: According to the laws of the former Yugoslavia, were you duty-bound to respond to mobilisation call-up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly, by all means. Every military-aged man is duty-bound to respond to a mobilisation call-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the consequence of avoiding mobilisation or not responding to mobilisation call-up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think a criminal report is filed. A criminal report is filed. There is criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, in terms of the reserve force that we're talking about over here, who are military conscripts? Are these two words synonymous, "military conscripts" and "reserve force"? Is it one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A military conscript and the reserve forces are not the same thing. Military conscripts are all of us, from the age of 18 to 60. Men, I mean. Well, afterwards, there was women too. I think that in the former Yugoslavia, for a given period of time, women were included as well. All are military conscripts, irrespective of what they did at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So what is the difference between the reserve force and military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we're all military conscripts. The reserve force are civilians. They are not engaged in the army. So a man who gets call-up papers and is mobilised becomes a soldier, and then when he is demobilised, he goes back to the reserve force. Again, he is a military conscript, but he's a civilian now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So military conscript actually includes the reserve force, the active force, and the military as such; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is general terminology.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, is taking an oath a precondition for a person to become a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Taking an oath is a ceremony that, in the Yugoslav People's Army -- well, I remember when I did that, when I did my service in the military in the former Yugoslavia, my parents came, and that is usually a ceremonial event, when your friends would come. I did my military service in Krusevac in Serbia because I came from Vitez, but I was not mobilised to the HVO. So then to take an oath does not mean that you have to take an oath in order to become a soldier. That has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you were mobilised, in your opinion, as you were taken to the front line on the 18th of March, 1993 -- I mean, the 18th of April, 1993. What did you get on that occasion? When did you receive weapons, equipment, a uniform from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that occasion, I did not receive a thing. What I had I took along with me, and I got a uniform, I can't remember exactly when, perhaps this was September or August. A month or two after I had joined the command of the company; that is when I got a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know where the weapons of the former Yugoslavia, rather, the JNA, were kept? Did military conscripts keep these weapons at home?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No way. When men would come back from the JNA, they would not bring their rifles with them. When you'd come back home, you'd just come with your military booklet. You would leave all your weapons and everything. You would be deissued.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That relates to weapons and uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Uniforms, weapons, badges, everything that you got when you went to serve in the JNA, you would have to leave. So, for example, when a person would come and when he would get various things from the JNA as well, then he would simply have to return all of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know where JNA weapons were held?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Oh, in barracks. Do you know which barracks? Around Vitez or in Vitez itself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Vitez, there was not a military barracks. There was only a warehouse at Slimena. I didn't even know about it at the time. I knew there was a military warehouse of the JNA, but what was in it, I did not know. Later, as things developed, we saw what was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: One of these warehouses was the one at Slimena; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. That is right, but that is the municipality of Travnik, not the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In relation to this and your status and your possession of weapons, we saw the film that was made by Professor Bringa. The Muslims say that the weapons they had they got as military conscripts from the JNA, the automatic rifles that they had, that they got that from the JNA. Was that possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I claim that it is impossible. Either that was the translation that was received or perhaps these people actually said it, but it's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, in relation to the military ID that is mentioned in (redacted) and that the Prosecutor asked you about, tell me, what did it look like? Can you describe it exactly? Can you exactly describe this military ID? Did it have a picture?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot remember it exactly, but as far as I can remember, it did have a picture, just like the military booklet, the ID from the JNA. I think there was a picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So there was a photograph in it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you thought that it was a replacement for the military booklet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the importance of this particular ID? What did it actually mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, what the importance was -- well, I don't know. I imagine that after the TO and the HVO were separated in Vitez, this was probably an attempt to see who was there and to abolish the old military IDs of the JNA and to issue something new. It was not similar to the military booklet of the JNA. The military booklet had a lot of pages and there were some instructions, et cetera, whereas this ID was just a single small sheet of plastic, I remember it was made in our company, and I remember it said "Member of the HVO." And what else did it say? I can't remember. But I know that my rank was not recognised from the Yugoslav People's Army, so it's impossible that it said "Commander." What it did say exactly, that I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You say that your rank was not recognised so it was not possible that it said "Commander." So what did it say?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it only could have said "Soldier" or perhaps nothing. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about the other members of the reserve force; did they have such IDs too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, everyone should have, but whether everyone did so -- well, at that time, I'm not going to say that paperwork was a travesty, but hardly any of it was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, was it indispensable for you to have such an ID? What did you use it for? What did you actually prove with it? Could you have done without that ID?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course I could have done without that ID. It didn't prove a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that you believed that it was issued to you sometime in the summer of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, approximately a few months before the first conflict. It was July or August. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, in July or August, when you say that it was issued to you, was there some kind of a military unit in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was an organised military unit, but I know that some had volunteered to go to Vlasic, to the front line against the Serbs. There were groups, I don't know, of about 20 or 30 people, I don't really know -- or I don't know who led them either. So I don't know that they were particularly organised at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which is the first military unit that was established in the territory of Vitez that you found out about, and when was this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was some kind of a Vitez battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the period of 1992 when this battalion joined the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, that is to say, Travnik and Vitez joined forces. I don't know when this was exactly. And sometime in 1993, again there was a brigade both in Vitez and in Travnik, Novi Travnik, and then the Vitez Brigade was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In connection with (redacted), you said that you gave your military ID, that you put your name on the door in order to protect her, that you spent the night at her place, and that that was the only way that you believed you could help her at the time and that is why you did that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps there were other ways of doing it, but I was not aware of any and she was not either. She did not propose anything either. I would have acted according to her proposal too, but we didn't know what else could have been done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At the time, in your opinion, and on the basis of what you saw was happening, that is to say, after these events in Ahmici and the knowledge that you had concerning events in Vitez those days, was it dangerous to help Muslims and why?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was dangerous. (redacted) herself told me, when I went to see her, that Croats who were helping Muslims in such a way had problems. She always told me about these people, about these unknown men in uniforms and black uniforms, the police, et cetera, and I said yesterday that, for example, if I were inside with my wife and children and if some men like that would barge in, how could they tell who was a Croat and who was a Muslim? I cannot say that there would be killing, but I don't know what they would be doing. They would perhaps be mistreating us. I don't know what they'd do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were you afraid at the time too? Did you think that it was dangerous?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These same men that (redacted) had described, and in addition to that, I saw people similar to that on the 16th and the 18th. Ivica Kupreskic said that these were the Jokeri. I don't know. I had associated them with that down there, although I had not seen it. I was afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me something else. You said that you came to the end of the review and you saw parts of the review in the summer of 1993 in Vitez and yesterday we also saw footage of a review from December 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, were there any differences between that which we saw yesterday and what you saw in August 1992 at the stadium in Vitez? Are there any differences between these two reviews?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were some differences. On this footage, I saw men in uniform, and most of them had weapons too, but in Vitez, this was not the case. There were quite a few without weapons and without uniforms. And I said that there were some men in blue uniforms, that was the Civil Defence; and then in white uniform, these were nurses. I did not see any of that yesterday in the footage we saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Several witnesses quoted by the Prosecutor yesterday referred to you using some military terminology, such as "commander," they would say a "local commander," "commander at Grabovi." Will you please look at these photographs, these aerial photographs? Will you please make small circles around the places which belonged to Grabovi? So will you please indicate the area of Grabovi?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean all the population, both Muslim and Croat?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So will you please tell us which area was usually referred to as Grabovi?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Marks). This.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So this then encompasses Kupreskics' houses, that area, and the Muslim houses around them.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In that area of Grabovi, how many of the houses were Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were four Kupreskic houses and two more but where the Kupreskic owners did not live in them, and there were two Vidovic houses, so six Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So two Vidovic houses which -- below that lower part.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm sorry. There was also a third Vidovic, Milka Vidovic's house, so three Vidovic houses and four Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And when somebody would say Grabovi, he would be confining himself to that area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes. In our local parlance, Grabovi would mean that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many Muslims and how many Croats were there in Grabovi?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the exact number of Muslims in Grabovi alone, but I should say it was three- or four-to-one. That would be the ratio roughly. I wouldn't know more exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How many Croats were there of military age, so men who could be what you call reservists or perhaps soldiers? In Grabovi, I mean.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Five. Five men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you please list them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Myself, my brother, Ivica, Ivica Kupreskic, Dragan Vidovic, Mirko Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And other Kupreskics were not there; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Right. So Abdulah Ahmic calls you a commander in the area called Grabovi, and all you have is five men.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was never a commander. I was a man who assigned guards sometime between the first conflict at the end of January, and then I returned and was just a play soldier and Dragan assigned guards after that. But nobody ever addressed me as a commander, neither of those soldiers or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But did you ever issue some verbal or written orders at any time before the 18th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that on the 20th of October, '92, almost all Muslims left the village. What did you mean by that? Does it refer to Muslims in Upper Ahmici, Zume Muslims, or Muslims from some other part of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I should say that I did not say almost all. The village of Gornji Ahmici, Upper Ahmici, or Pirici, nobody left on the 20th of October. They all stayed home. People who lived nearer to the gunfire left, that is, Muslims around the school and the mosques and those Muslims who lived closer to my place, and we, the Kupreskics, left too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In relation to the agreement, D27/1, which the Prosecutor showed you yesterday, that was the agreement which features your signature, you recognise also the signatures of other participants to that agreement. Would you know if there is another Fahrudin Ahmic in the village apart from Fahrudin Ahmic who was Mirjan's friend?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There's another Fahrudin Ahmic who also lives there nearby, near the road, and his name is Fahrudin Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Fahrudin Ahmic's signature, I mean, the one who was killed? Have you ever seen his signature?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I may have, but if I saw such a signature now, I wouldn't be able to say "Yes" or "No." I wouldn't be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So could you really establish whose signature it is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In relation to the events of the 20th of October, that is what you said in your testimony, but in several places it is directly quoted and mentioned the way in which the roadblock was removed. Do you know how this barricade was lifted, the one that was on the road near the sub-trail on the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All that I know about the removal of that barricade is that it was a military action of the soldiers who came from Busovaca and peasants, that it was a military defeat of men who were manning the roadblock, the Muslims. There were no negotiations about how to remove it. It was removed by military action.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: As for the ceasefire, was that negotiated or did the Muslims simply withdraw?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The fire stopped around 3.00 or 4.00 on the 20th, that is, when the gunfire stopped, and not a single bullet could be heard after that, and some negotiations began a day or two later. I said already one thing about that, not about the ceasefire, that is, but how to bring the tension down, and the gunfire had already stopped before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In relation to the testimony of Witness Y which was referred to by the Prosecution and he said that you allegedly asked, as a local commander, that you asked the Muslims to discontinue their guard duty. As a local commander of Grabovi, were you vested with any kind of authority that the Muslims should and would respect?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They did not have to respect whatever I said or did, but they could, of course, because we were friends, we knew one another, and I did say yesterday what were my words at that meeting, and I was not asking or requesting the Muslims not to go on guard duty. I mean, who was I, what was I to tell them not to do that? I was talking, Let us not be on the road. I mean, why not go on as we did before?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But were you in a position to order Muslim guards anything?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I couldn't order anything, my guards anything, let alone Muslim guards. All I could do was kindly ask any of my guards to go out and stand guard. If he refused to -- well, I could go on trying to prevail upon him to go, to agree to it, but apart from that, I could do nothing, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe this would be a good time to take a break, because in the second part, I will want to show some documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, still in relation to

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: things more. Tell us, in your answers to introductory questions of the Prosecution, namely, whether all the Muslim houses in the village were burnt down, you did not mention that there were also some Croat houses demolished. Why didn't you mention those houses, and do you know that some Croat houses were also burnt down that day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not mention it because it seems to me insignificant. There were Muslims and Croats victimised that day, but Croat houses were also damaged. All the Croat houses were damaged, window panes, roofs, and so on. Dragan Vidovic's, Mirko Vidovic's, and many other houses were damaged. All the houses near the scene of the fighting were damaged, but it was really minor. There were also two houses in Pirici, Gavro Vidovic's old house and his sister's summer cottage in Gornji Pirici, Upper Pirici. In Zume, there were also a couple of houses that were damaged by shells. But I repeat, it was such minor damage or, rather, it simply does not lend itself to comparison with what happened to Muslim houses, so I simply thought that what -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Didn't you say that there were two houses which were intact near the Kupreskics houses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Were there some houses intact along the road going through Zume?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those houses which were intact in Pirici, I don't know whether three or four houses, but Ramo Bilic's, Zijad Bilic's, and their brothers, I believe his name is Asim or something like that, he lives in Vienna but he built a house up there, and the Strmonja sons lived in those houses. All these houses are intact. I know that two or three Muslim houses intact are near my sister's house in Santici belonging to Serif Ahmic and his son, Ljilja, or something like that. Their houses are also in one piece.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: These Bilic's houses, where are they exactly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They are in Pudzine Kuce. As we go from our houses to the Pudzine houses or towards the Vrebac's shelter, we must go by those houses. They are on our way there.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: How many times did you walk past those houses on the 16th, 17th, or 18th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I went by some ten times altogether, going there, coming back.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Their inhabitants were Ramo Bilic and his family and the Strmonja families. They were in Anto Vidovic's shelter; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is, yes. It is some 40 metres or so. It is across the road where Niko Vidovic's shelter was.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Do you know who roused those people, who woke them up that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know who woke them up in the morning, whether Niko Sakic or Jevco. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Do you know if Niko was the one who prevailed upon them to go to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: You also said that after the first conflict on the 20th of October, 1992, there were several reports about Mujahedin attacks from Barin Gaj. Were you in touch with people in Ahmici, with Muslims in Ahmici in relation to those reports and used in your family's transfer to Zume?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can remember one occasion when we moved out our families in the evening, around 9.00, I don't know, to Zume, to that Vrebac shelter. It could have been earlier. Then we came back to near the stable or behind my uncle's house where we usually spent our time on such occasions and that Fuad Berbic had called by telephone my uncle's house where my aunt was. She never went anywhere, she was always there in Ivica Kupreskic's house, and she called me to tell me that Fuad had been asking for me. Judging by his questions, somebody must have let him know that the Kupreskics and their families should go to Zume, and Fuad was calling to ask me what it was all about, Fuad asking me. I said that we'd heard that there were Mujahedin and that we should go with the children, and he was telling me, "Oh, come on, Zoran. There's nobody there. Wait. I'll let you know if anything." And I said, "Fuad, I do believe you and I don't, but what's to it? I can go to Zume and come back." Indeed, an hour or two later, he called again to say that he'd made a round and there was nothing there, and, indeed, nothing was there. That is what I remember. It was after the 20th of October. It could have been some 20 days later, perhaps a month after that. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: On such occasions when you went to take your family to Zume, which road would you take?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We always took the shortest possible route from our house, by my uncle's house to Niko Sakic's, because that is the shortest route.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Why didn't you use that route through Ahmici towards the road and then following the road to the other side, to Zume?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because that is too far, because that is simply too long. From the Muslim side, there would be reports of an attack, and then we simply wouldn't dare take it, but we used to take the shortest route.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Was this one of the reasons why you did not use the car?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Ivica and Dragan Vidovic had cars. He would need two or three minutes to Niko Sakic's house, if he was using the road, and if you wanted to use the car, then you had to go back to the main road. It would almost take more time to go there using the road. So I didn't use it and they didn't use it either.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Let's say in the situation when your children were to be transported, your parents, you had three small children, some personal effects, wouldn't it have been more convenient if you used the car?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As I said, it would have been more convenient, but we didn't do it. We would have to go through part of the village where the Muslims were, and if there were Mujahedins there to join them, if there were any foreigners there, we didn't know whether there were any soldiers there so -- for instance, in Barin Gaj, like on the 19th and 20th, when Ivica saw it there, that was our first experience of this kind. Bullets were raining, not at my brother and my own, but this is how we felt. Based on this experience, I did not dare stay at home in the same way as I did on the 20th. So based on that experience, I would use the shortest way, rather than go around through the Muslim populated area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we should go into private session at this point. I need to mention a name (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, let me ask you in conclusion: You've been sitting here for already a year now. You have been listening to the course of this trial, you've been listening to witness statements, and some of them have indeed levelled terrible accusations against you. Tell me, what do you think about this? What is your experience of this? From an emotional point of view, how have you been following this trial and how do you explain all of this to yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN KUPRESKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Through superhuman effort and strength, I try to remain calmed, composed, but not wishing at any point in time to underestimate the victims of Ahmici because indeed the Muslim people had suffered there. I was not there. There is not a single move that I made that I reproach myself for, at least I cannot see anything of that kind, and I do not want to underestimate in any way the suffering of those poor people there, my neighbours. However, this war has fundamentally changed my life. My mother has -- myself, my brother, and our sister -- she lost her husband, our father, she lost her brother, she lost 15 close relatives, and now she lives on her own in Ahmici on a pension of 100 marks. I'm practically a refugee. I have been a refugee until I received an apartment from my company. My wife had terrible problems. A year ago, she underwent surgery. Psychological reasons led to this surgery, and she can have no more children. Two of my children got ill. They suffer from bronchitis, a disease which is very difficult to cure, and my wife pays 200 to 300 marks per month for medicines, and she is thanking God for the fact that our children have started recovering from this illness; otherwise, it takes a long time for it to be treated. Our eldest son has just completed the seventh grade. He's an adolescent. At that age, children wish to have a great many things, and it is very difficult for her to raise him the way I had been raised. I was raised in a patriarchal Christian family. I got a Christian upbringing: Think no evil, let alone do an evil. For 15 years, I've been doing yoga, which teaches one not to harm animals or plants, let alone human beings. For 20 years, I have been friends with people of different professions, different backgrounds, different ethnic backgrounds, religious backgrounds. I never had any conflict with any man except a conflict of opinions. I started talking about my eldest son. Our eldest son has started making trouble. He started lying and doing this and that, and it is hard on my wife. She cannot cope with him on her own and I cannot help her. When some witnesses were here and when they were pointing their fingers, my heart wanted to jump out of my body. However, I am prepared to do anything to prove that I am innocent. And I am available to the Honourable Court at any point in time, at any moment, I am ready to answer their questions whenever. That is what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Kupreskic. We have concluded, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kupreskic, I have a few questions, but I would like to go into private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your microphone is still on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, are you going to call another witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic, could you please take the stand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration? THE ACCUSED MIRJAN KUPRESKIC: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kupreskic, could you please introduce yourself to the Court, and would you tell us where and when you were born, what your address is?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to apologise because I have a bit of stage fright. My name is Mirjan Kupreskic. I was born on the 21st of October, 1963 in the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What is your address? What is your residence in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: You mean at the time when I was born? I lived in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm asking now, about the last address you had.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Now it is Petra Svacica. I don't know exactly the number of the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You were born in Pirici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I was born in Vitez and I lived in Pirici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You went to elementary school in Pirici or, rather, Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It was in Ahmici, four years of elementary school in Ahmici, and then I went to the elementary school in Stanica, up to the eighth grade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you complete secondary school and where?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In 1978, I completed the eighth grade, and I got a scholarship from the company Slobodan Princip Seljo in Vitez where our father was employed. I got this as an exemplary student and probably thanks to my father and his work. I had received a scholarship from this company, and I went to work Trstenik to be trained as a technician.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where is Trstenik? How far away is it from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Trstenik is about 400 kilometres away from Vitez. It is in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You spent four years there, and after that, what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In 1982, in the summer of 1982, I completed my education and I went back to Vitez. Two months later, I immediately got a job in the Slobodan Princip Seljo factory, since I had had their scholarship, and I was supposed to have a job of this kind; however, I got a job as a mechanical technician rather.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How long did you work in the SPS, until when?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I worked in the SPS until the beginning of 1992 when I went on leave. This was the end of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the meantime, in this period from when you got a job until you went on leave in 1992, what did you do? Were you in the army? Did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In 1982 when I got a job and until April 1984, I mean, then I went to the JNA, and a year later, I came back, and then I got a job at the same company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you get married in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In 1987, I got married to Ljubica. Then, her maiden name was Vrebac, and now her last name is Kupreskic. In 1987, we got a daughter, Marija, on the 6th of September, and three years later, on the 6th of September, our son Marko was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After you went on leave in February 1992, after that period, did you work anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: After 1992, the financial situation was very precarious, critical. All my revenues boiled down to music, to this orchestra of mine that was there together with me. So financially, I depended on music entirely, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you get a job somewhere officially?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Sometime in August, I don't know exactly when this was, 1992, my cousin, Ivica Kupreskic, opened a wholesale company, and he asked me whether I would like to take care of this wholesale business. Given this financial crisis that we were undergoing, I wholeheartedly embraced this offer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This was in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, second half of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Until when did you work in this company?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I worked there until the 15th of April, 1993. During the war, I did not work, and immediately after the war, when I was demobilised, I returned to that job again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This wholesale business that belonged to the Sutra company, where was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: This wholesale business where I first started working was in Ahmici. This was a newly built building, and it was owned by Vlatko Kupreskic. That's where I worked perhaps some ten days before the war broke out because Ivica's plan was to open a new big wholesale business in the town of Vitez itself, where the retail store was, and right next to this retail store was a big building where he wanted to open this bigger wholesale business, and I was supposed to take over this facility. I was supposed to take care of all these goods, and it was all supposed to go through me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In other words, some ten days before the conflict, you moved to the Vitez store?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I moved from the wholesale to the retail outlet, and expecting that the wholesale business would begin to operate fully, I started to work for this retail outlet because formally, the saleswoman who worked there had some other obligations, and she left the store, so I took over.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When did you resume your work for the Sutra company?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: You mean after the war? I think it was sometime in April 1994 when I requested to be demobilised, and so I was -- rather, as soon as it started working, I was back there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After April 1994, did you ever put the uniform on again?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: After April 1994, no. No, I did not put the uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you were born in Vitez but had been living in Pirici ever since your birth. The first village -- Pirici comes immediately after the -- adjoins the Muslim village of Ahmici. So you've lived in the vicinity of Muslims all your life and lived there?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I've lived in Pirici in my old parental home ever since I was born. I went for the first four grades of elementary school in Ahmici, and all my neighbours and all my school fellows were Muslims together with me. All the children who were there, we all moved for the senior four elementary grades to Dubravica, so we were all together once again. After the eighth grade of elementary school, I went to Trstenik with Asim Berbic, who was my neighbour, and he spent all four years in Trstenik together with me. We shared a room with two beds. We never separated for a single day during those four years. Let me make it clear. He is Junuz Berbic's son, and Fuad Berbic is his uncle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So Asim Berbic, with whom you spent those four years and shared a room in the hostel, is a Muslim; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was your parent's attitude to Muslims? How were you brought up?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can say that my parents had more friends among the Muslims than among the Croats. I could name here the majority of those neighbours who, at a time when I was a young boy, of course, I wasn't there when I went to school, but again after I came back, I saw them, and as far as I saw it, the majority of those neighbours were Muslims, and they were on very good terms with my folk.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What Muslims were close friends of your parents? Who are they?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can say that about Alaman Ahmic, who moved in at some later late. I do not think that a day would pass without the late father and him playing cards or being together, and Niko Sakic who joined them there. Then Redzib Ahmic and his wife were often in our home, and my parents often went to visit them. Mehmed Hrustanovic, Mejo, Mehmed, I don't know exactly. Zarfa and his wife were also on very close terms with my parents. Then down next to the mosque, Hilmija Ahmic and his wife were also on very good terms with my people, and often we visited one another. Then the hodza of Ahmici, he was also on good terms. Fahrudin Pjanic and his wife Rosa were on exceptionally good terms with my parents. I can't remember if Muhamed Ahmic and Vahida Ahmic, I think she was my mother's bosom friend. They never separated. I could go on and on with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: These people, Redzib Ahmic and Hrustanovic, they are all people from houses next to yours; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Hrustanovic and Redzib Ahmic lived nearby. Alaman Ahmic has his house closest to our house, and Hilmija Hazim and Muhamed Pjanic, they are a bit further way. They are around the mosque, that cluster of houses around the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about Sakib Ahmic? He is your parents peer. He was also your neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could mention Sakib Ahmic like those others, except that there were times when Sakib -- that was his conduct, and I'd heard, I mean he was rather prone to drinking alcohol, so he would keep apart. But there was no major strife.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But from time to time, would there be any trouble with Sakib Ahmic, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, indeed, there were some misunderstandings about the boundary, because my father had it with him, and my brother and I and the younger generations paid no attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How did they socialise? They are people of more or less the same age. What did they do together?
