utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I already said, Alaman Ahmic, for instance, I said that hardly a day would pass without him playing cards. They mostly played cards together. They also had their own topics, which only they knew. They went on holidays, for instance, on a Croat holiday, then they would come to pay us a visit, and, likewise, if it was a Muslim holiday, then we would, of course, return the visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The younger generation, what did you do and what terms were you on with Muslims and how did you socialise?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: When I was a child, I would often go with my parents to those visits, but then as time went by and we grew up, then, of course, we led a different kind of life or, rather, there was a kind of modernisation. We would not go to each other's houses. We met somewhere around the town, in cafeterias and around there. Some true, real friends, some topics brought us together or simply life brought us together, and it was only then that we went to one another's houses. But it was just life and the kind of work that sometimes took us apart. We had less time for any house calls.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you got married and the rest of them married, were you best men to one another?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, particularly those of us who were together in this folklore company, and we were together. Yes, of course, we were best men to one another, and, of course, we married between us. I could mention three or four marriages which were the product of that friendship in that folklore company.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You mean marriages between Croats and Muslims; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Between Croats and Croats, and Croats and Muslims, and Croats and Serbs. They all intermarried, all variations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: One group of people, apart from those in the village, was this a group of people from the folklore company with whom you and Zoran frequently met and socialised for awhile?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Most of the people who were in that company were friends. Yes, of course, we were friends with them, and naturally, there are people who are much closer to you, and then that friendship grows into something higher, into something better. But I was a pal with all of those people who are in that company. With some of them, I was very close friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who were those closest friends?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Fahrudin Ahmic, the late Fahrudin Ahmic. I don't think I should waste any words about that. He was not only a friend from the folklore company, but he was also a man who was in the band with me together, that is, we had various things that we did together, which brought us together. So in the orchestra, in the band beside him, there was Nedzad Barucija who was a singer, another Muslim. I must separate them now into Muslims, Croats, and Serbs. I never did that before, but now I have to do that. Now, as far as Nedzad Barucija is concerned, I need to say that it was thanks to me that he made a cassette, recorded a cassette. Perhaps he would have never recorded it had it not been for me who somehow introduced him to those people who sang and the orchestra. There was also Mustafa Dzidic who danced in the folklore and Amir Sivro. There was also Ibrahim Salkic, another dancer, Veljko Cato, who was my best man, and he's a Serb. Miro Vujinovic, another Serb, and he was also my best man. He was with the orchestra, not with that orchestra that we were in the folklore company but another band that was a semi-professional orchestra. I could go on and on naming various people. These are the ones that just come to my mind right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did any changes happen in your relations after the first conflicts in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can say that after that first conflict, that those -- that it may have brought us even closer together. Because of all those events, we simply did not want anything like that to affect us in any way, and we were all very eager to come even closer together in view of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened with the relations amongst you after the war? Do you keep in touch with your Muslim friends?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: After the war, I received an information, I don't know exactly how I got it, I did not mention a number of people, I did not mention somebody else. Naim Mekic from Kacuni, I just forgot him. Throughout the time our semi-professional orchestra existed he was a singer, semi-professional, and I learned that he was inquiring about me, whether I was alive and what has happened to me. I believe that it was Zdravko Vrebac who told me that he had been inquiring about me. After I learned that, I went to Zdravko and told him, "Well, why don't we go in the car and go to Kacuni?" Because Kacuni was separated. There was this checkpoint in Kacuni at that time, and Zdravko agreed, so we got into the car, I switched it on --- and I don't remember it was three or four months after the war ended --- and I remember we got in the car, and we got a crate of beer with us to take it to Naim's. We got to this checkpoint and Muslim policemen were at that checkpoint there. Most of those people recognised both me and Zdravko, because when we played, I would often go to Naim or Naim would come to me, so those people knew me because we simply socialised with that music. So when I turned up at that checkpoint, these people welcomed me very cordially and asked me, "Are you going so that Naim and you can play once again?" I treated them to that beer which we had with us, and so they said, "We will go and look for Naim. You wait here, we are sure to find him, so don't move anywhere." Some 10 or 15 minutes later, they came back, and they told me that they had found him and to wait and that he would come, and then another 10 or 15 minutes later, we met, and it is really very hard to describe that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That was when?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, I did say I'm not quite sure, whether it was March or April 1994, that is, as soon as all that fighting ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact or were you in touch with other Muslims after the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: When I began -- when I resumed my job at the wholesale in Vitez up there, it was a country -- when was that? Was it in 1994, perhaps 1995, when Mustafa Dzidic and I did say that -- he was our close friend in the folklore company. He came to me, he came to the wholesale, to Veleprodaja, and I saw him there. Otherwise, before that, when we were friends, when we were bachelors, and after that, we were trying to dress properly, to look after what we wore and how we would appear. Then on that occasion, when I saw this man, he really looked very wretched. It would be hard for me to describe what he looked like. We talked. It was our first meeting after the war. He told me that he was in very dire straits financially. I knew about his house which I, my brother, and other friends were building together with him. We were there to place the concrete foundation, and I knew that he had a very convenient space in his house, in the lower part of his house. During that conversation, it occurred to us that perhaps he might try and open a shop down there and that I would try with Ivica to take over part of our merchandise because at that time one could open a retail shop for about 2.000 or 3.000 marks and start quite a successful business with that. Perhaps he even came on that occasion to see if we could help him. So, anyway, we talked, and then it occurred to me that perhaps I might try to do something. So I got in touch with Ivica and I told him that, and Ivica said, "Well, you know that man well. You're his friend, and I'm not going into that, but if you are backing that, then you will guarantee that, because after all, you are responsible for all that merchandise." I assumed the risk, and I cannot say if the merchandise that I offered to put at his disposal was 2.000 or 3.000 marks. I put it in my vehicle because I had a car, that was the first time I had a car, I never had a car before, and in a trailer, I then took it to Stari Vitez, to the old part of the town where his house was, I took all this merchandise there. After that, he came on a number of occasions, and we agreed that he would pay for that merchandise as he sold it, gradually. So at times, he would bring 100 marks or 150, 250, depending on how he operated and how he managed. So he would return 100, 200 marks, and then take again another batch of goods. Until the time when I came here, whether it was 1.000 or perhaps 1.200 marks that he still owed me, I don't know. I never saw him again. But I know that he was still due me that part of the debt for which I am responsible, that is, I have to pay that money back. But let it be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Apart from those people, did you socialise with some other people, with some other Muslims, after the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can say about Ahmed Delic, he's a younger bloke and he used to dance in the folklore company before the war and after the war and even during the war when we once tried to have a concert for Christmas, but we failed because of all that was happening, and immediately in the wake of the war, Ahmed Delic joined the folklore company again, and we absolutely made no difference -- I mean, it was the same before the war and after the war, even though he is younger than I am and we were not all that close, as with Mustafa Dzidic and some others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You socialised with these people at a time when you realised that the indictment was issued against you?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to them, if I may just add regarding the contacts – (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You don't need to mention the name. It is Witness CB.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness CB. I remember, that was also in 1994 in the summertime, my wife and both my children had left for Split because both of my children have eyesight problems. So she went there to have them examined and get them eyeglasses. I came back home, it was late, between 11.00 and 12.00, and the phone rang. I picked up the phone, and the witness was on the phone. For a couple of minutes, I was stunned. I didn't know how she could have found the phone number. I didn't know where she was. I must say, I sat down in the hallway. I could not stand on my feet. I did not know how she was able to find me and how she summoned strength to do so. We talked. First it was about this friend -- she cried more than talked. And during this conversation, we both expressed our desire to see each other and meet, and I don't know how much time had passed, 15, 20 days, I came in my car to Gavrine Kuce, between Zenica and Vitez, and very little traffic went back and forth. She said that she would come to this checkpoint by bus and that I should come in my car to pick her up. I did so and then drove her back to my place, and we stayed there for several hours. I did not know of a single Muslim who had come to Ahmici after the war which took place. She may have been the first ever.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, at that time, in some media, on the radio or in some papers in Zenica, your name was being mentioned in connection with these crimes?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, it is true, and it wasn't only my name that was being mentioned but all the Kupreskics and all the neighbours who were Croats, and at that time, she also said that she had heard about it and she obviously did not believe it because she would not have come to visit me and stay in my house. So I was the first person whom she contacted after all this because we were true friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the conversation you had with her, did she at any time complain about your not having saved her husband that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: At no time did she ever mention it nor did we ever arrive at that issue of my being able to save her husband, and she never asked me any such question, whether I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Regarding the people whom you mentioned that you socialised with before and after the war, we tried to contact some of them and attempted to have them come over here to testify as witnesses. What is the problem in their not coming here?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically what the problem may be, but perhaps pressure for these people to say who were the perpetrators and then perhaps pressure not to help us. I did not believe in truth that it would come to this, that I would be tried here, but when I got here and when I realised what was going on, I tried, through you, to contact some of these friends to provide statements about me, and you tried too, and you know what you succeeded in getting. They said what -- and you can say what they did when contacted the first, second, or third time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Of the two persons you mentioned, we received character statements, Mustafa Dzidic and Naim Maric --

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- do you know why they are not able to come here and testify before this Tribunal what type of person you are? Do you know whether they have problems? Did they say? Do you know of their having problems about coming here?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't have specific knowledge, but when you first talked to Naim Maric, you know that he cried when he spoke, and after that he said that he was prepared to do anything. I don't know whether later on there were threats or something, but he was not prepared to sign the statement. As far as Mustafa Dzidic is concerned, you talked to him, and at first he said that he would testify by video link regarding my character, but then he decided to just sign it; and when it came to signing it, he said that he was afraid. I don't know whether they were threatened, but everything leads me to believe that these people have received some threats. These people know me and my brother, and knowing them as much as I do, given what we have done for them, I think that this is the least that they would have done, give this type of character witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that in February 1992 you were laid off at the SPS where you had worked, that at the time you had no financial means to support yourself.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in 1992, I think it was in February, I was temporarily, provisionally laid off, as most people in SPS, and the only way of my getting any financial means was through playing music and dance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So in addition to being part of the folklore group, you also had an orchestra, a band that you played with?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I have to make a distinction here. We had a folklore group, and that was -- I did it out of enthusiasm. I was also an accompanist with a group. Until 1991, Nail Kacar, who was a professor of music in Zenica, I was an accompanist after he left to go back to teach full time, and myself, Fahrudin Ahmic, and Zdravko Vrebac were the only three steady musicians. There were two additional musicians who would join us if we had larger performances. So Zdravko Vrebac, Fahrudin Ahmic, and I were the only permanent musicians. We also then had a semi-professional group, band, and I partly supported myself with that, and those three, Ivo Jandric, Miro Vujinovic, a Serb, and then Naim Mekic would sometimes join us as additional musicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did your wife work at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No, she never worked and even today she is not employed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the only money you ever received at that time you received through your work as a musician?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the money that I ever received in that period of time, until I started working for the wholesale Sutra, was from music.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, you started with the village guards in the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this was in February or March, but these village guards were established. I don't know how this happened. I know that Zoran told me. He asked me whether I wanted to join in, and I said, "Sure. Why not?" But I said that if I had enough time because this was a period when I played, and I played in the evenings, and these guard duties were nightly duties. So whenever I could, I would go and stay on that guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: According to the witness statements, it would seem that only several persons were doing this guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: You mean in the very beginning? As far as I know, when I first started doing it, I was together with Mirko Vidovic. At first we said, "Why don't you pair off with whomever you feel comfortable, with whom you share some interests?" And so this is what we did. At that time, Ivica was not around, he had gone to Germany. Sometimes Mirko Sakic, Miroslav Pudja, Nikola Samija, Drago Grgic, I think that Miro Vidovic and Miro Samija were also involved. So altogether, about ten persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, given your involvement in music, did you have problems in keeping up with guard duties every night with those ten men? So if you were only about ten, then you pretty much would have to appear there every night?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Given the number of persons, everybody would have to take a two-hour shift. Whenever I did not play, of course I was on guard duty, but when I did, that was a priority because that was the only means of support. Sometimes if I would stay up well into the night playing, then obviously I couldn't go out on guard duty the next night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Until when did this guard duty go on in your village?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I can only speak about myself. They went off and on until the first conflict, and at that time, we were there at that barn, and then for a month, it was interrupted again. I cannot name every interruption, and I don't know if there were 10, 15 days or a month, I wouldn't come out for several days, but I know that there were a number of interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Can you say whether there was an assignment sheet made for every night of duty?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no assignment sheets. The first time I went out was with Mirko Vidovic because we agreed to pair off together, and the agreement was -- I think it was 10.00 to 12.00, 12.00 to 2.00, so if we were out 10.00 to 12.00 first night, then the second night would be 12.00 to 2.00 and then the following night 2.00 to 4.00 and then 4.00 to 6.00 and then start all over again. If I did not come out for the guard duty, if it coincided with my playing engagement, then for those two hours, nobody would come out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What type of weapon did you bring with you to the guard duty?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: At first, during the initial period, it was a rifle which was the property of Mirko Sakic, it was a hunting rifle; and after that, Miroslav Pudja also brought in a -- I think it was an automatic rifle. So those were those two rifles which were used for guard duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have your own rifle?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I did not have my own rifle. Only in December when Didaks, who came as refugees from Turbe, moved into Ivica Kupreskic's brother's house, Zarko Didak gave me an old M48 rifle because he had used it previously at the front line against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When he gave you that rifle, did he also give you some ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: He gave me two boxes. There may have been ten rounds apiece per box that went with that rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I did not have a uniform. Sometimes if it rained or if it was cold, Zoran had received a camouflage blouse or a top, a jacket, and it's water-resistant, he received it from someone, so I would sometimes borrow it from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you receive one from the HVO later; that is to say, after the war broke out, did you get some other equipment or weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: While I was at the front line during the war above Ahmici, in the trenches, I personally did not get a rifle, but in the trenches there were better weapons or such weapons. So they remained in the trenches, and those were the weapons that I used while I was up there in the trenches. Also some uniforms were handed out, jackets, depending on who got what.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This guard duty went on until the first conflict, you said?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the first part?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: They went on until the first conflict with these brief breaks, as I said, but they were rather loose, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you know how guards were organised on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I did not know how they were organised, but I knew that they had guards too, and that before this part of ours, when we started standing guard, that they and part of Zume had already been standing guard. While we were standing guard, we would often be together with them. We would walk along this road towards the school, especially Mirko and I, when we were on guard duty, we would like to stop by at the elementary school where one of their radio transmitters was. And I mentioned Nedzib Ahmic, who was an elderly man and a close friend to my late father and mother, he was a very interesting man, very witty, and sometimes he would be at that school. Mirko and I, when we were on duty, we would like to go down there immediately because then the two hours would go by quickly. He was a very interesting man, very witty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When were there problems in connection with your going to the school?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On one occasion -- well, I cannot say this was a problem, but we would often go to the school and we were at the school, and as far as I can remember, Sefik Pezer was there most of the time because he was trained probably as to how to use this radio transmitter, and a few other people, I can't remember exactly who was there because they actually asked us to leave because they were supposed to transmit something via radio, and that was a sign to us that we were not supposed to hear what they were supposed to report. After that, we were embarrassed to go to the school, and that's why I didn't stop by there anymore, and I told either Zoran or, I don't know who else, that that is what we were told. After that, we avoided stopping by. We did it rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What is this kind of radio transmitter that they had at the school?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about this big (indicating) and it had antennae. I don't know exactly whether this was an RUP; it was olive grey-green. Yes, that was the colour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What about your guard patrols? Did they have any radio transmitters?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: None whatsoever. I am not aware of any such thing in the part where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You say that was not a problem, but let's say that this was a lesser incident, when you were asked to leave the school. After that, did Croat guards stop by that school or did you stop with this entirely?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I think that no one stopped by at the school, no one entered the school, but we still walked along that road. We would again see each other, spend time together. I personally, when I was with Mirko, after that time I did not enter the school. Whether somebody else had entered it after I did, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you have any other obligations in addition to going out for guard duty? Were you engaged elsewhere at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, for example, Civil Defence.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, no. As far as the military part is concerned, guard duty or whatever, no, I was not engaged anywhere else except for this guard duty, which I accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In relation to the events of the 20th of October, 1992, can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber whether you had any knowledge that this conflict would break out? Did you notice anything on the 19th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of October, it was a normal day to me, like any other day. I worked at the wholesale outlet. I met all these people; people would come in to buy goods. After I finished work on that day, I remember that, with Zoran and Dragan Vidovic, I went to help him to bring in some wooden boards. I know that on our way back, we came across this checkpoint that was at the entrance to the village. It had been placed there earlier on, and I remember when I went out for folklore rehearsals or when I went out to play music, it was not directly on the road. People stood by the road. It was quite normal. We would say hello. They did not stop me. And I saw that evening too. However, on our way back, there was this wooden device in the middle of the road, and we simply said hello. Nothing happened. They removed this wooden device. I saw a few neighbours from the village. There were a few people who were not from the village, who were unknown to me. There were different uniforms; some people had uniforms, others did not. Some had rifles, others did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The checkpoint that you're talking about is the checkpoint that was on the road to Ahmici; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the road that leads from the main road to the road to Ahmici, some 20, 30 metres along that road. There was a garage there, a shed of the late Sakib Ahmic, the one from the road, and then near that shed, there were some elements that were placed, and also there, there was a cover, a nylon cover if it would rain. So people moved there anyway. But that evening, this wooden device, so to speak, was put in the middle of the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This checkpoint was held by the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: In twilight on the 19th, these men I saw were Muslims, the ones I knew; and the ones I did not know, I can only assume who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you said that, a few days earlier, this barricade on the road was present, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it was not placed on the road, it was next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The men from the village, the Croats, the people from the village, were they bothered by the fact that somebody was checking up on them and that a checkpoint or a roadblock was being put on the part of the road that leads to their village?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, personally, it didn't bother me because it ensured my safety too, that somebody would be checking on who was coming in, because I lived there too, after all, and there was quite a bit of crime at the time. So they are taking care of me too, they are guarding me too, if you look at it that way. Whether it bothered someone else, that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: The other roadblock that was by the Catholic cemetery, did you find out about it on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: On the 19th, I did not know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That night between the 19th and the 20th, did you go out on guard duty?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I did not. As far as I can remember, that night, I went out to play some music, and in the morning, I opened the shop and I worked down there. I hadn't slept much. I helped Zoran with the wooden boards, and I could not go out for guard duty that evening. It turned out that during the night, they called me, and again, I spent part of the night until the morning out there although I had so little sleep. So that's the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who called you?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Zoran telephoned me, and he said that he was at Ivica's and that I should come to Ivica's too. I don't know exactly what time it was, day had not broken yet, and I found Zoran at Ivica's, and Ivica told me what he had seen, and he already conveyed that to Zoran, that he had seen a group, 20 or 30 men, who had passed from the upper part of Ahmici by this warehouse, the wholesale, and that he saw them get into the school. When I was there, you could already see in the direction of the school -- Ivica's terrace is pretty high up and you can see the school quite well -- and in part of the classroom, there was a light that was on, so you could see the silhouettes of persons. He said that he saw two men below Zoran's window, which worried us the most at that point. Partly it was worrisome because of the time when they came. They used to come earlier too and they would go from the school to the front, to Visoko, I don't know exactly where they went to, and this was either during the day or twilight, but this, this was during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You saw them during the night and you heard them pass through your village. Did you wake up your family?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I did not see them. Ivica told me that he had seen them, and I saw in the school what I described to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: But I did not wake up my family at the time. They were asleep at home, but we decided to stay awake, Ivica, Zoran, and I, to see what all this was about, and that's how we were up until daybreak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What happened at daybreak?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: At daybreak, I remember well that we were sitting on Ivica's terrace, and there was always a table with plastic chairs on Ivica's terrace, and that's where we sat. This was the usual time for the morning prayer from the mosque, and when I went to work to the SPS, that was the time when I would leave, and that is when this morning prayer could be heard. That morning, it was different in relation to every other morning. There was a kind of -- well, it was like the gurgling of a brook. It's hard for me to describe, but I could notice that it sounded different from what it sounded like all the other mornings. Also, you could hear something being said. I could not understand what was being said, but something was being said. Just when these words stopped, there was a strong detonation. I remember how we jumped up from the detonation. On Ivica's terrace, there was some kind of a rug, and since this was a concrete terrace, that's why they kept the rug, and then as I jumped up, I remember that I slipped on the rug and I fell, and then we ran into the house. Then there was a complete lull in what we had heard. I can't tell you whether this was 15 or 20 minutes or up to half an hour. I remember that my late father came, because he was probably awakened by this detonation, and he came there to see us, and after a certain period of time, the late Enver Sehic came, who was our next-door neighbour, he lived right next door to my house, that is to say, just above my house, and 7 or 10 days before that, Zoran and I went to help Enver to bring in firewood. So on that morning, he was supposed to help me, or perhaps it was the other way around - I can't remember exactly whether we had already taken care of my firewood and we were supposed to take care of his now - and he came to see whether we would be going to get this firewood or not, because of this detonation that had taken place, so we stayed there together. An hour or an hour and a half later, after this detonation, this strong small arms fire began which was right above our houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How could you assess the direction from which the shooting came? Did you hear shooting or what?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We heard shooting, and it was coming from down below, that is to say, from the road, from the cemetery, from that part, and the bullets, we could have estimated that they were flying above our heads, but I don't know exactly how far away. I cannot judge the distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could you see Croat or Muslim soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I could not at that point. At that point, when the shooting started, I ran to my house and I told my wife to get the children ready so that we would flee, and at that point, I didn't even know where we would flee. I returned from my home once again, and then I saw Zdravko Vrebac. He was running up to me, and he addressed me as "Kum" because he was the godfather of my small son Marko, and he came to help me. He did not know what was going on. We went to my house. He took Marko or Marija, I can't remember who my kum picked up, but I was carrying one of my children and he was carrying the other one; and under this host of bullets that were flying above our heads, we literally ran into my uncle's house, and we hid there for about five or ten minutes, until there was a lull in the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your uncle's house, that is the house of Ivo Kupreskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You spent some time there until there was a lull in the shooting, and then where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I forgot to mention something else. That Dragance, as we called him, Dragan Vidovic, helped him, and Milutin Vrebac. They were together with Zdravko Vrebac, when he came, so they helped Zoran so that he could take care of his children. So we were all there together in my uncle's house until there was a lull in the shooting. When there was a lull in the shooting, then we managed to get to the depression that we passed through, and I took my children and my wife also came with us to Zdravko's house -- to Zdravko Vrebac's sister's house, rather, where there was a shelter that they used before that, and then Zdravko, since he had come to see me, then we went there together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. We know what happened on that day. Tell me, what did you see out of all these things that were taking place? Did you see civilians, soldiers? Did you see who was attacking who?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Who was attacking who? That, we could not see. During the course of the day, we could see from the lower part that -- from Zume, part of the Muslims were running towards Gornji Ahmici, the upper part, and they were bringing some of their cattle along, and there were women. We were at Niko Sakic's, near the depression, in my uncle's house, and if we were at Niko Sakic's, then we could see the lower part. Or if we would go close to the shed, through this part of the forest, you could see part of the warehouse and the road that went up. So we could see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you did go up to this shed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: We were in that part between the shed and the depression and Niko Sakic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In addition to the civilians who were fleeing, did you see any military men?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I did not see any military men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You and your neighbours, your neighbours who were there with you, did you use weapons in any way on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely no one used any weapons, and in that group of these people who were there with us, perhaps there were two or three rifles, I don't know, we had used some of them on guard duty, and whether there were some other rifle, that, I don't know, but absolutely no one used a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there any combat activity in your part of the village?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And in Zume?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And the people who were in that depression on the 20th, that is to say, you and your neighbours, were you in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall whether somebody had a camouflage jacket or whether somebody had had a full uniform. It depended on who was on guard duty and depending on who had worn what on that morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: According to you, when did the gunfire stop? When do you think you heard the last bursts that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: As far as I could judge, it was in the afternoon hours. Whether it was around 3.00 or 4.00, I wouldn't know, but it was in the afternoon. In the afternoon hours was when the gunfire ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What did you do after that? Did you go back home?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Some five or six days later, when all our neighbours had gone back, my brother and I and our families and our parents also went back because our families were the only ones from the Kupreskics' houses, my wife, my children, Zoran's wife and his three children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How old were your children at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Marko, my son, was one year old, and Marija was four.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the negotiations conducted on the return of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I know that Zoran attended a meeting at Nenad's home, that then he went with Fuad down. As far as I know, the only reason was the return both of our families home and of our neighbours home, because to spend the night, unless there is someone in your house or around your house, was very difficult under the circumstances. So that the only reason was the return both of us and of our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What were you afraid of if the houses around you were empty?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, if you live alone in some part somewhere and there was gunfire the night before or during the day, then it's very difficult really to be so brave and spend the night alone in the house with one's wife and small children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you thought that you could be attacked?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what I thought at the time. I was simply afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And those other houses, Kupreskic houses, apart from yours and your father's, Zoran's, Ivica's, and Vlatko's houses, they were all empty, were they?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Ivica's brothers' houses, Branko and Josip's houses, were completely empty because they were both in Germany; that is, Branko had gone to Germany, it must be some 15 years before that, and Josip left, oh, towards the end of '91 or '92, had also gone to Germany, and there was a third brother, Ranko, who did not have a house of his own, he lived over at his uncle's, but he was also in Germany; and their sister, Marija, was also in Germany. So Ivica's family was in Germany and Ivica was the only one who was at home in his house at that period of time because he had come back, and then myself and Zoran with our families and parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After you returned home, you said it was about five or six days after the conflict. Did any changes take place there in what you did, I mean, night guards?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: I know that at night, but whether it was on the 20th or 21st, I don't remember exactly. We agreed, because of all that gunfire, that we really should begin to take this guard duty seriously. I believe that I was exposed to the harshest criticism because I was often absent from that duty, but it was force majeure at the time. I mean, I had to play music and all that. But we all said that we should take it more seriously, as I know we told Zoran that he should also pay more attention, that is, if anyone failed to appear, then somebody else should turn up instead, you know, to cover for those two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was another, a new checkpoint perhaps set up at the entrance into the village?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: When you ask me about those negotiations, I was not present at any of those negotiations nor did I take part. I don't really know whether I -- why I was absent. Had anyone asked me to attend, I probably would have, but I know that nobody ever asked me to attend. However, I do know about a meeting, if one can call it a meeting, which took place on Ivica's terrace because it was right after that meeting, whether the same day or the next day, Ivica came to my place and said that they had agreed that that checkpoint, which I described already which was at the entrance into the village, that they had agreed that now we, together with our Muslim neighbours, should be there, the two of us. I said that -- he said, "I agreed to be the first one to man it," so would I join him? And I said yes. So he and I were the first ones there. There was also a fellow who testified here, I won't mention his name, he was also with me and with Ivica, and as far as I can remember, Sidik Ahmic was there because his house is right next to the road there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the understanding, that both Muslims and Croats should man the checkpoint together, is it --

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, two each.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, two Muslims and two Croats. For how long was this checkpoint in operation?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: That was the first time I was there, and after that, I didn't go there again. But as far as I know, perhaps a week later, it stopped functioning, that is, I don't know that anyone manned it after that, neither the ones nor the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Which means that the checkpoint was removed, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But the guard duty went on, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, the guard duty was as I said it, that we should take -- we decided to take things more seriously, and perhaps we did. But, I don't know, it could have been a week later when I began to work again, I mean, for that wholesale, and I was still again busy with that job, and people began to go back to their regular work because the situation became more stable, if I may put it that way, so that people relaxed somewhat and then discontinued it. At that time, in November, I was very busy at this wholesale place because at that time we were distributing winter preserves which the Sutra company got and was distributing to all the citizens in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: This distribution of winter food supplies or winter preserves, it was an organised campaign to supply all the population in the Vitez territory at cut-down prices; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was an offer that came from the manager. It was accepted at the municipal level. I didn't know that. I didn't go into that. But I know it was accepted and that I bore the brunt of that distribution of those winter supplies because I was put in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you began to do it sometime towards the end of October and you said on the 1st of November, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in late October, early November. As soon as the wholesale unit went back into operation is when we began doing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So these winter supplies and preserves were also intended for Muslims, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: They were intended for everybody, regardless of their ethnicity and whoever applied for this. It was done by neighbourhood communities who compiled lists or whatever, but whoever applied for those winter supplies got some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, did you visit Muslim villages around Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MIRJAN KUPRESKIC
utterances.text: Well, we began to distribute those winter supplies at the wholesale unit too, that is, some people came to the premises and would get their share, and sometimes we also took it to parts of villages, whether they were Muslim or Croat. I know, for instance, specifically that Ivica and I went to Sivrino Selo and distributed it at Muharem Sivro's because he was the president of the neighbourhood community or something. Before that, he used to work in the same company with me. We were in his house where we distributed those winter supplies, and he was one of those who received some of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
